lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Owned the claims backlog report and the weekly numbers the claims managers used.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Wrote the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Improved reporting efficiency by 90% by moving the monthly revenue report to scheduled SQL queries.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.
- Wrote data-quality checks on the 40 most-used tables, catching 15 broken loads before they reached a dashboard.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Reported the national conversion rate as the simple average of 14 regional conversion rates, without weighting by regional traffic.
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Compared the forecast with the operator's rebalancing schedule: empty-station hours fell from 310 to 205 a week in a replay of last summer.
- Published the notebooks and a short write-up, which the city's open-data team linked from its bike-share page.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Built a retention dashboard for about 2.4 million shoppers that raised repeat purchases by nearly a quarter.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: Date of birth and nationality are included in the résumé.
items.because: They are conventionally omitted and can distract from qualifications.

items.says: Experience is not ordered newest-first.
items.because: Brightcart is more recent and senior, but Pinecrest appears first.

items.says: EDUCATION appears before EXPERIENCE.
items.because: Leading with the degree delays the candidate’s more relevant analyst experience.

items.says: The claims-report bullet does not show the reporting work performed or a measurable result or enabled decision.
items.because: The reader cannot evaluate the work’s analytical skill, scale, or operational value.

items.says: The call-center analysis does not identify the method behind the staffing recommendation.
items.because: Without the method, the recommendation is harder to assess as analysis rather than an unsupported conclusion.

items.says: The strongest call-center outcome should appear earlier in the entry.
“My findings” uses a personal pronoun.
The halving of query errors has no baseline count or measurement period.
items.because: The reader cannot judge the reduction’s scale or how long it lasted.

items.says: The fraud-automation result is buried among unrelated support duties.
items.because: It is unclear which work saved 10 hours a month, and the list reads like general support rather than analytical ownership.

items.says: “Reporting efficiency” does not identify the 90% metric, and the repeated “by” is hard to scan.
items.because: Without a clear metric and baseline, the percentage is difficult to interpret or trust.

items.says: The join is reversed and cannot find customers with no orders as written.
items.because: Starting with orders excludes those customers, while a null customer name indicates an unmatched order.

items.says: The finding gives neither the number of customers found nor the decision it enabled.
items.because: The bullet reads like an isolated query exercise rather than work whose retail value is clear.

items.says: The data-quality checks do not specify what they tested or how they stopped broken loads.
items.because: Without a representative validation, the reader cannot assess the quality-engineering work.

items.says: The bullet foregrounds presenting rather than the analysis or recommendations behind the funded outcome.
An unweighted average of regional rates is not generally the national conversion rate.
items.because: The national rate requires total conversions divided by total traffic, or a traffic-weighted average.

items.says: The calculation gives no purpose, correction, decision, or consequence.
items.because: The reader sees a technical calculation but no demonstrated business value.

items.says: The retention-dashboard bullet should open the entry.
items.because: It contains the clearest quantified business outcome.

items.says: The retargeting clause makes it ambiguous who performed the retargeting.
“12% mean absolute error” misstates the metric unless it was normalized.
items.because: Mean absolute error uses the target’s units; a percentage needs a defined denominator and a relative-error label.

items.says: The forecast result does not show what changed because of the forecast.
items.because: Without a connection to an action, the project reads as model production rather than applied analysis.

items.says: The accuracy figure has no validation period or baseline comparison.
items.because: The reader cannot judge whether the error is strong or what data was held out.

items.says: The modeling approach is not identified.
items.because: Python and SQL show tools, but not the forecasting technique behind the result.

items.says: The line wrongly credits comparing a forecast with a schedule for reducing empty-station hours.
items.because: A comparison cannot change availability; the reduction is claimable only if a replay applied forecast-guided rebalancing.

items.says: The line does not explain how the forecast changed the rebalancing schedule.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what decision rule or inventory action was simulated.

items.says: The rebalancing result should open the project.
items.because: It is the strongest impact line.

items.says: “Fell from 310 to 205 a week” makes the unit and comparison hard to parse.
The publication has no measure of reach or reuse.
items.because: The city link shows recognition rather than an enabled outcome.

items.says: The line treats the shorter Saturday line as caused by mapping visits.
items.because: The map cannot establish that the shift change caused the reduction; other factors could explain it.

items.says: The candidate’s personal contribution to the team analysis is unclear.
items.because: The team-of-three entry does not show whether the candidate mapped visits, interpreted the findings, or helped implement the change.

items.says: “Moved one volunteer shift” does not specify the schedule change.
Matching repeat visitors does not by itself yield a count of unique households.
items.because: Household membership requires identifiers or a validated matching rule separate from matching visitors.

items.says: The line gives neither the count produced nor how the pantry used it.
items.because: The 9,000 logs describe source size, not the matching result or a decision it informed.

items.says: The retention-dashboard bullet does not fit the pantry project and duplicates Brightcart’s achievement.
items.because: Its shoppers and repeat-purchase outcome describe the retail work, not the pantry visit logs.

items.says: The repeat-purchase increase lacks a comparison baseline and the candidate’s contribution is unclear.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what the increase was measured against or what analysis or action linked the dashboard to it.
